ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fixation-Dependent Intent Questions on Egocentric Cooking Recordings
PROPOSAL: Build a multiple-choice benchmark from the EGTEA Gaze+ cooking recordings, with 1200 questions about the object the wearer fixates, the next action and its reason. Three annotators confirm that no question can be answered without knowing the fixation point. Evaluate a seven-billion-parameter Qwen vision-language model and an eight-billion-parameter InternVL model zero-shot on sampled frames, once without gaze and once with the fixation drawn as a coloured circle, and report accuracy by question type with bootstrap intervals.
CONTROLS: Guessing from the question text alone to expose language priors; a circle placed at a random frame location to test whether any marker helps; a circle at the true location taken from a different clip to test whether the benefit is specific; human accuracy on a 100-question subset.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Accuracy without gaze stays close to the text-alone level on fixation questions and rises clearly with the true circle, while random markers give no gain. It could fail if annotators leak gaze-free cues into the questions, and the gap would then shrink.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze-Conditioned Intent Questions on Kitchen, Workshop and Street Video
PROPOSAL: Assemble a benchmark of 3000 multiple-choice items drawn from EGTEA Gaze+, Ego4D and Aria recordings, covering fixated objects, next steps, motives and scene layout. Three raters score how strongly each item depends on gaze, a fourth settles their disagreements, and a second round rewrites ambiguous ones. Test four open vision-language models from three families on sampled frames, at three frame counts, with and without a coloured circle at the fixation. Report accuracy per question type with bootstrap intervals.
CONTROLS: Blind question-only prediction; a marker at the frame centre; the true marker borrowed from a neighbouring clip; rater accuracy on 300 items spread over the three corpora, with agreement between the raters.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Accuracy without gaze stays near the blind level on fixation items and rises with the true circle in each corpus, while centre markers give no gain. It could fail if camera motion differs so much between corpora that pooled results mask opposite trends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze-Cropped Visual Tokens for a Video Assistant
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model so that, besides global frame tokens, it receives tokens from a high-resolution crop around the fixation point. Train with LoRA on 40000 gaze-annotated question-answer items built from Ego4D and EGTEA Gaze+, using a frozen visual encoder and a trainable projector for the crop branch. Evaluate on held-out fixation and intent questions, reporting accuracy per question type and tokens per frame.
CONTROLS: A copy of this model fine-tuned on identical questions with global frames alone; a crop centred at a random point; a crop at the true point but with gaze coordinates shuffled across clips; the untouched model prompted with a drawn circle.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The crop branch beats the global-frame fine-tune on fixation and intent questions by a clear gap and beats the circle prompt by a smaller one, while random crops fall back to the global-frame level. It could fail if the gain comes from resolution alone, which the random-crop control would reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zoom-Level Gaze Tokens with Full-Model Training for a Video Assistant
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a thirty-two-billion-parameter vision-language model so that it receives, with the global frame tokens, tokens from three crops of growing size centred on the fixation. Update every attention layer and the projector on 160000 gaze-annotated question-answer items from Ego4D, EGTEA Gaze+ and Aria, and retrain from scratch under three learning rates and four initialisations. Evaluate on held-out fixation and intent questions, reporting accuracy per question type and tokens per frame.
CONTROLS: A global-frames-only fine-tune on the same items; crops centred on a random point at each size; true crops paired with gaze shuffled between clips; the original model prompted with a drawn circle; a single-size crop for comparison with the three-size design.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The three-size crop design beats the global-only fine-tune on fixation and intent questions, with the largest crop contributing little beyond the middle one. It could fail if one size dominates, so that the other two add tokens without accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: How Well Do Current Models Read Intent Without Gaze
PROPOSAL: Measure zero-shot intent understanding on 400 egocentric clips from EGTEA Gaze+ without any gaze input. For each clip, write one question about the current goal and one about the next step, then score a seven-billion-parameter Qwen vision-language model and an eight-billion-parameter InternVL model on four uniformly sampled frames. Break accuracy down by whether the target object is held, near the hands or just visible in the background, and report intervals.
CONTROLS: A blind baseline that sees just the question; majority-answer prediction per question template; a human annotator who watches the clip without gaze; and a model fed the correct narration to bound what perception alone can reach.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Models perform well above chance but below humans, with the largest deficit on clips where the target object is in the background. It could fail if question templates leak the answer, which the blind baseline would show as unexpectedly high accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intent Reading Without Gaze Over Wearer Activities and Clip Lengths
PROPOSAL: Score zero-shot intent understanding on 1500 egocentric clips from EGTEA Gaze+, Ego4D and Aria, with gaze withheld throughout. Four questions per clip cover goal, next step, preference and reason. Six open vision-language models are tested at four frame counts. Results are split by activity, by clip length and by the position of the target object, whether held, near the hands or in the background, with intervals around each cell.
CONTROLS: Question-only prediction; the most frequent answer per template; two people who watch the clips without gaze, on 300 clips; the correct narration supplied as text to bound what perception alone can reach.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Models perform well above chance but below people, with the largest deficit on background objects, and model ranking stays stable across frame counts. It could fail if activity effects dominate and swamp the object-position effect.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Choosing a Gaze Presentation Format for Video Language Models
PROPOSAL: Compare four ways of presenting gaze to a pretrained eight-billion-parameter vision-language model: a drawn circle, a blurred-surround heatmap, a cropped view around the fixation, and fixation coordinates written in the text. Run each format zero-shot on 2000 fixation and intent questions from EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, then fine-tune the best two with LoRA for one epoch. Report accuracy, and the drop caused by shifting gaze by a fixed distance.
CONTROLS: No-gaze prompting as floor; formats applied at a random location; a text format with coordinates rounded coarsely; and the fine-tuned model evaluated with gaze removed to check that it actually uses the signal.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Cropped and heatmap formats beat the circle and the text coordinates, and fine-tuning widens the gap. It could fail if all formats help equally after fine-tuning, so format choice would matter for the zero-shot setting alone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze Presentation Formats: Colour, Width, Size and Precision Variants
PROPOSAL: Study nine presentations of gaze for three pretrained vision-language models: circles in three colours, a blurred-surround heatmap at two widths, crops at two sizes, and fixation coordinates written in the text with two precisions. Each is tried zero-shot on 9000 fixation and intent questions drawn from EGTEA Gaze+, Ego4D and Aria, after which the best four are fine-tuned with LoRA for three epochs. Report accuracy and the drop when the fixation is shifted by assorted distances.
CONTROLS: No-gaze prompting as floor; every format placed at a random location; a circle in a colour missing from the scene; and the fine-tuned models scored with gaze removed to confirm that they rely on it.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Cropped and heatmap formats beat the circle and written coordinates, and fine-tuning widens the gap on all three models. It could fail if colour or width choices move accuracy as much as the format family does, which would blur the comparison.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Teaching Gaze Reading with Synthetic Gaze-Grounded Instructions
PROPOSAL: Because training data rarely contains gaze, build 25000 synthetic instruction items from Ego4D narrations by pairing each narrated action with the fixation recorded at that moment and writing one of three question styles that names the fixated object merely implicitly. Fine-tune a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model on them with LoRA, then test on a human-written benchmark of fixation and intent questions from EGTEA Gaze+. Report accuracy per question style and the change on questions that need no gaze.
CONTROLS: A model fine-tuned on matched items without gaze; items whose gaze is paired with the wrong moment; the base model with a circle prompt; and a check on a general video benchmark to detect forgetting.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning on gaze-paired items lifts accuracy on fixation questions above the circle prompt, with no loss on gaze-free questions. It could fail if the model learns narration style rather than gaze, which the wrong-moment control would reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze Instruction Data at Four Mixing Fractions from Three Narration Sources
PROPOSAL: Since pretraining corpora seldom include gaze, synthesise 120000 instruction items from Ego4D, EGTEA Gaze+ and Aria narrations, linking each action to the fixation recorded then and writing five question styles for it. Train a thirty-two-billion-parameter vision-language model with LoRA on four fractions of the items and test on a human-written benchmark of fixation and intent questions. Report accuracy and change on questions needing no gaze.
CONTROLS: Matched items without gaze; items with gaze paired to the wrong moment; the base model with a circle prompt; and three general video benchmarks to detect forgetting after each fraction.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Accuracy on fixation questions rises with the data fraction and passes the circle prompt, with no loss on gaze-free questions. It could fail if the gain saturates early, in which case the larger fractions add nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sensitivity of Gaze Benefit to Tracker Error
PROPOSAL: Corrupt the recorded fixation of 1000 EGTEA Gaze+ question items with Gaussian offsets of four sizes, from small to a sizeable fraction of the frame, and with random dropout of fixation samples at three rates. Present the corrupted gaze as a circle to an eight-billion-parameter InternVL model and measure accuracy on fixation and intent questions. Fit a curve of accuracy against offset size and locate the point where the gain over no-gaze disappears.
CONTROLS: The clean-gaze result and the no-gaze result as ceiling and floor; offsets in a fixed direction versus random directions; and temporal smoothing of the corrupted gaze to test whether noise averaging recovers the benefit.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Accuracy declines smoothly with offset size, and the benefit vanishes once the error approaches the typical object size. It could fail if the model ignores the circle at all offsets, so the curve is flat and the clean benefit was small.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze Benefit Under Tracker Error and Lower Sampling Rate
PROPOSAL: Perturb the recorded fixation of 4000 EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D question items using Gaussian offsets at ten magnitudes and random loss of fixation samples at seven rates. Show each perturbed gaze as a circle to three vision-language models and measure accuracy on fixation and intent questions. Fit accuracy as a function of offset and dropout rate, and find where the gain over no-gaze vanishes for each model, listing the largest offset at which that model still beats the no-gaze floor.
CONTROLS: Clean-gaze and no-gaze results as ceiling and floor; offsets in one fixed direction against random directions; smoothing over windows of three lengths, to test whether averaging restores the benefit.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Accuracy declines smoothly with offset and dropout rate, and the benefit vanishes once the error nears the typical object size on all three models. It could fail if the curves lie so close together that the finer grid separates nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze-Aware Pretraining of a Video Language Model
PROPOSAL: Continue pretraining a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model on a corpus of 300000 egocentric clips with recorded gaze, adding a gaze encoder whose output is injected into the visual token stream by cross-attention. Train in two stages: the encoder alone, then the full model with LoRA. Evaluate on fixation and intent questions from EGTEA Gaze+ and report accuracy, together with attention mass placed on the fixated region.
CONTROLS: Continued pretraining without the gaze encoder; the encoder fed shuffled gaze from other clips; a circle prompt on the base model; and a general video benchmark to check for regressions.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The gaze-injected model beats the circle prompt and the no-encoder pretraining on fixation questions and shows more attention on the fixated region. It could fail if continued pretraining alone, without gaze, produces most of the gain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Four-Stage Gaze Encoder Training for a Video Language Model
PROPOSAL: Extend the pretraining of a seventy-two-billion-parameter vision-language model on 900000 egocentric clips with recorded gaze, inserting a gaze encoder into each layer of the visual token stream by cross-attention. Training runs in four stages: encoder only, encoder with projector, full model with LoRA, and a final full-parameter pass. Evaluate on fixation and intent questions from EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, reporting accuracy, attention mass and the share of heads that attend to the fixated region.
CONTROLS: Identical pretraining with no gaze encoder; the encoder driven by gaze shuffled between clips; the base model with a circle prompt; general video benchmarks to detect regressions.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The gaze-injected model beats the circle prompt and the encoder-free pretraining on fixation questions, with more attention on the fixated region. It could fail if the first two stages deliver all the benefit and the later ones leave accuracy unchanged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Auditing Whether Questions Truly Need Gaze
PROPOSAL: Before any model comparison, audit a draft set of 600 egocentric questions built on EGTEA Gaze+ clips. For each question, run a text-based classifier, a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model without gaze, and that model again with a drawn circle, and record whether the answer changes. Have three people attempt 150 questions with and without a gaze overlay. Retain the questions whose answers change just under the overlay and report how many survive.
CONTROLS: A shuffled-label baseline for the classifier; questions rewritten to name the object explicitly, which should remove the gaze dependence; and agreement between the two people measured with a chance-corrected statistic.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: A sizeable share of drafted questions are answerable without gaze, and explicit rewrites remove the gap, confirming that the audit detects dependence. It could fail if people use the overlay as a hint at the answer, so that retained questions are biased toward easy ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Screening Draft Questions from Three Sources for Gaze Dependence
PROPOSAL: Screen a draft pool of 3000 egocentric questions written on EGTEA Gaze+, Ego4D and Aria clips. Every question goes to a text-only classifier and to five vision-language models, with the fixation circle and without it, noting whether the answer changes. Four people attempt 900 questions with and without the overlay at two time offsets. Keep the questions whose answers change only under the overlay and report the survivors per source and per question type, with the loss between screening rounds.
CONTROLS: A classifier trained on shuffled labels; rewrites that name the object explicitly, which should remove the dependence; agreement among the four people measured by a chance-corrected statistic.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: A sizeable share of drafted questions are answerable without gaze, and explicit rewrites remove the gap in all three sources. It could fail if the five models agree so closely that they tell us no more than one model would.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fixation Sequences Versus a Single Gaze Point for Intent
PROPOSAL: Test whether the temporal pattern of gaze carries intent beyond the current fixation. On EGTEA Gaze+, build 1500 questions about what the wearer will do next, and give an eight-billion-parameter InternVL model either the current fixation circle, or the trail of the last three seconds of fixations drawn as connected markers. Fine-tune each variant with LoRA on a disjoint training split and report next-action accuracy by the number of distinct objects visited.
CONTROLS: A no-gaze fine-tune; a trail with order of fixations randomly permuted; a trail from a different clip; and a frame-based model given the next frame as an upper bound on visual evidence.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: The trail helps most when the wearer visited several objects before acting, and permuted trails lose most of that benefit. It could fail if the single fixation already carries nearly all the signal, so that trail and circle tie.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze Trails at Longer Prediction Horizons for Wearer Intent
PROPOSAL: Ask whether gaze history predicts intent at longer horizons. From EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, write 6000 questions on the wearer's next step, next minute and next scene. Three vision-language models receive either the present fixation circle or a trail of the last two, five or ten seconds drawn as linked markers, and each variant is fine-tuned with LoRA on a disjoint split. Report accuracy by horizon and by number of distinct objects visited.
CONTROLS: The no-gaze fine-tune; a trail whose fixation order is permuted; a trail from another clip; a frame-only model given the next frame as an upper bound at each horizon.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Trails help most for the next step after several objects were visited, and permuted trails lose that benefit. It could fail if the benefit disappears at the longer horizons, where no fixation trail predicts what comes next.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: End-to-End Test with Estimated Gaze in Place of Recorded Gaze
PROPOSAL: Train a gaze predictor on EGTEA Gaze+ that estimates the fixation from video and the wearer's hand positions, then feed its output as a circle to a fine-tuned seven-billion-parameter vision-language model. Compare accuracy on 2000 fixation and intent questions when the model sees recorded gaze, predicted gaze or no gaze, and report the share of the recorded-gaze benefit retained by the predictor.
CONTROLS: A predictor that always outputs the frame centre; a predictor trained on shuffled labels; recorded gaze degraded to the predictor's own error level; and a held-out kitchen split to measure generalisation of the predictor.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The learned predictor retains a substantial share of the recorded-gaze benefit and clearly beats the centre predictor. It could fail if the predictor is accurate just on frames where the object is already obvious, so that its benefit is small where gaze matters most.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Estimated Gaze from Three Predictor Families at Three Capacities
PROPOSAL: Train three gaze predictors on EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, each at three capacities, that infer the fixation from video and hand positions, and pass their output as a circle to fine-tuned vision-language models of two sizes. Compare accuracy on 8000 fixation and intent questions under recorded gaze, predicted gaze and no gaze, and report the share of the recorded-gaze benefit kept by each predictor at each capacity, with intervals.
CONTROLS: A predictor that always returns the frame centre; a predictor fitted on shuffled labels; recorded gaze degraded to each predictor's own error level; a held-out kitchen split to measure generalisation.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The learned predictors keep a substantial share of the recorded-gaze benefit and clearly beat the centre predictor, with capacity mattering little beyond the smallest. It could fail if predictors from all families make the same errors, so that comparing them reveals nothing.
